items.answer: Empirical study is a usability-testing stage in interactive system development, performed after code testing, that systematically tests a fully implemented system with end users through a controlled experiment to collect and analyze data for assessing overall usability.

Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert usability inspection method in which evaluators identify problems by performing interface-level tasks converted from a scenario on at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype, guided by usability questions framed in advance.

Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to identify usability problems across the whole system at an early design stage.

Integration is a stage of the tracking process that aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to combine the values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment, and computes the current sensor orientation from the initial orientation estimated during registration and calibrated angular velocity samples.
Interaction design is the activity of designing user input in an XR system from the user's point of view to make the user's interaction easy, effective, and seamless.
Iteration is a cycle that returns to a previous stage of interactive system development to account for user feedback, in which a design is prototyped, evaluated, and refined until it is stabilized.

questions.question: During requirement gathering for an interactive system, which group is the primary source of usability requirements?
options: Design teams
Clients
Testers
End users
questions.explanation: Usability requirements are collected mainly from end users, while functional requirements may come from both end users and clients and other non-functional requirements may come from clients.

questions.question: Which observation indicates that an interface design is stable?
options: Further evaluation is unlikely to produce many new issues
Further design is unlikely to produce many new issues
Further coding is unlikely to produce many new issues
Further prototyping is unlikely to produce many new issues
questions.explanation: Stability is reached when further evaluation is unlikely to reveal many new issues. Further design, prototyping, or coding is not the stated stopping point for the interface design cycle.

questions.question: Why does an interactive system need an empirical study even after its code has been tested?
options: Code testing shows documentation, not usability
Code testing shows executability, not usability
Code testing shows requirements, not usability
Code testing shows usability, not executability
questions.explanation: Code testing establishes that the system can run, but it does not estimate how usable it is, so an empirical study is still required.

questions.question: What makes a long path to deployment possible in the traditional interactive system development lifecycle?
options: Each phase is reviewed and documented before the next phase starts
Each phase is prototyped and documented before the next phase starts
Each phase is coded and documented before the next phase starts
Each phase is completed and documented before the next phase starts
questions.explanation: Deployment is delayed because each phase has to be completed and documented before later work can begin, so any delay or paperwork accumulates. Requirements such as coding or prototyping do not apply to every phase.

data.text: The traditional interactive system lifecycle proceeds through requirement gathering, interface design, code design, implementation and code testing, and an empirical usability study. Each stage must be fully completed and documented before the next stage begins, so deployment comes only after all requirements, design, coding, testing, and usability work are done. Because stages take time and require separate documents, this strict process can produce time and cost overruns or client non-acceptance.
points: Requirement gathering collects functional, non-functional, and usability requirements from clients and end users.
Interface design uses repeated design, prototyping, and evaluation cycles until the design is stable.
Code design is produced through iterative brainstorming and design notations.
Implementation's coding and code testing show executability, not usability, so an empirical study with participants tests usability.
Long stages, strict completion, and documentation can delay deployment and cause time/cost overruns or client non-acceptance.

questions.question: What is the main delivery difference between agile development and standard ISDLC?
options: Agile waits for the completed system before any delivery
Agile keeps delivering features over successive deliveries
Agile keeps collecting requirements over successive deliveries
ISDLC keeps delivering features over successive deliveries
questions.explanation: Agile adds features and delivers them in successive releases, while standard ISDLC completes the system before delivery. The other options reverse or misstate this delivery pattern.

questions.question: Why can an agile sprint run for four to six weeks while a full ISDLC can take six to nine months?
options: A sprint does not try to test the release
A sprint does not try to collect feedback
A sprint does not try to train the users
A sprint does not try to do everything at once
questions.explanation: A sprint is short because it works on a limited part of the system rather than the whole project. Testing, training, and feedback are still part of agile work.

questions.question: How does an agile team use demonstrations and feedback inside a sprint?
options: It demos the current iteration and shares quick feedback for the next cycle
It demos the final system and shares quick feedback for the next cycle
It demos the current backlog and shares quick feedback for the next cycle
It demos the current iteration and shares written feedback for the next cycle
questions.explanation: Agile teams give a live demonstration after an iteration and use quick stakeholder feedback before the next sprint. The wrong options replace the demonstrated iteration or the quick feedback with something not used that way.

questions.question: What is the stated purpose difference between agile methods and standard ISDLC?
options: Agile targets documentation completeness, while ISDLC targets quick stakeholder feedback
Agile targets hardware feasibility, while ISDLC targets user training
Agile targets the overall flow, while ISDLC targets practical products
Agile targets practical products, while ISDLC targets the overall flow
questions.explanation: Agile methods are presented as a practical way to build acceptable products, while ISDLC is mainly a pedagogical model for understanding the overall flow. The other options swap or misassign those purposes.

questions.question: What sequence of work happens inside an agile sprint?
options: design, prototyping, empirical study, and deployment
feasibility, documentation, coding, and maintenance
conceptualization, inception, release, and production
requirements, development, testing, and delivery to production
questions.explanation: An agile sprint moves from requirements to development, then testing, and then delivery to production. The wrong options mix in surrounding lifecycle stages or stages from other development models.

data.text: Agile development is contrasted with the standard Interactive System Development Life Cycle (ISDLC) as a faster, more incremental way to build interactive systems. Instead of completing everything first, it works through short sprints that each move requirements, development, testing, and delivery forward. Daily meetings, demonstrations, and quick customer or stakeholder feedback let the team adjust the next sprint, which supports practical delivery rather than only a textbook lifecycle.
points: Agile development starts small, cuts unnecessary documentation, and aims for quick, client-acceptable projects.
Agile development delivers features over successive short sprints, unlike ISDLC's one completed delivery.
In the agile process flow, a sprint includes requirements, development, testing, and delivery.
The agile development team uses daily meetings, demos, and quick customer and stakeholder feedback to shape the next sprint.
Agile methods aim at practical acceptable products, while ISDLC mainly explains the overall lifecycle flow.

items.title: Order the stages of the agile development process
steps: The team is created and funds and resources are arranged
The product is developed through iterations or sprints
The release is tested, trained, documented, and deployed
Ongoing support and maintenance are provided in production

items.title: Order the activities in an agile sprint
steps: Requirements are chosen from the backlog and stakeholder feedback
The developed work is tested with training and documentation
The tested work is delivered to production

questions.question: What purpose do the recommended human-computer interface design and implementation materials serve for a learner?
options: They support deeper study of visual perception, auditory design, full immersion, and resource optimization
They support deeper study of prototype building, prototype evaluation, empirical study, and agile methods
They support deeper study of usability testing, code testing, turnaround time, and development cost
They support deeper study of requirement gathering, interface design, code design, and system implementation
questions.explanation: The additional materials are meant for going deeper into prototype building, prototype evaluation, empirical study, and agile methods. Earlier lifecycle stages, perception topics, and testing or cost-related concerns are not the focus of that recommendation.

data.text: Further study of implementation concepts is directed to the Human-Computer Interaction book and NPTEL course weeks 4, 5, and 10 to 12. These sources are recommended for concepts such as prototype building, prototype evaluation, empirical study, and agile methods. They give the learner a place to extend the implementation-stage ideas.
points: Use the Human-Computer Interaction book and NPTEL weeks 4, 5, 10-12 for prototype building, evaluation, empirical study, and agile methods.

questions.question: Why does the traditional interactive system development lifecycle often delay deployment and risk client non-acceptance, whereas agile sprint-based delivery can be quicker and more acceptable?
questions.reference_answer: Traditional deployment waits until requirements, coding, code testing, and usability testing are all complete, and each stage must be fully completed before the next. This rigidity can cause time and cost overruns and non-acceptance. Agile development starts small, keeps delivering by adding features over successive deliveries, and a sprint is shorter because it does not try to do everything.

questions.question: Why does an interactive system still need an empirical study even after implementation and code testing have shown that it is executable?
questions.reference_answer: Implementation consists of coding followed by code testing, which can show that the system is executable. However, code testing does not show whether the system is usable. An empirical study, also called usability testing, systematically evaluates usability with end users, so it provides the usability evidence that executable code testing alone cannot provide.

questions.question: How does an agile sprint use customer or stakeholder feedback to keep development iterative and user-centered?
questions.reference_answer: In a sprint, requirements are based on the sprint backlog and on customer or stakeholder feedback, and the team provides a live demonstration after each iteration. Quick feedback is shared with the team before the next sprint so that it can be addressed. This creates iterative loops in which user needs and expectations can redirect the work instead of forcing a fixed stage sequence.
